newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Ashland, Marathon link part of broad shakeup.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ashland, Marathon link part of broad shakeup.

text.p: Thursday's news that Ashland Inc and Marathon Oil Co will marry their U.S. refining interests by the end of this year is part of a broad shakeup of the global "downstream" oil industry, analysts said.
"This is an industry trend that began two and a half years ago with Mobil (Corp ) and BP (British Petroleum Co) in Europe," said Fadel Gheit, an industry analyst at Fahnestock & Co in New York.
"There are now a lot of couples either married or engaged in the industry but there are still a number of single and unattached players looking for a partner," he said.
Among the most eligible still looking are Amoco Corp, Atlantic Richfield Co and Sun Co, said Gheit.
Indeed, there is hardly a company in the industry which is not at some stage of negotiation for an alliance, partnership or merger, analysts said.
"I'm sure there will be more to come. I think everyone is thinking, reviewing and deciding which partner to join with," said Jack Aydin of McDonald & Co Securities Inc.
The long-term implications for the industry are dramatic.

"This thing will shake out in the next couple of years and the whole shape of the industry will change, so you'll end up with a bunch of large players with strong geographic market share," said Ravi Kamath, an industry analyst at Jeffries & Co in Houston.

The move toward regional concentration already is apparent, and the Marathon/Ashland link-up will create a concern with about 25 percent market share in the Midwest, though that shouldn't cause any anti-trust problems, said Gheit of Fahnestock.

The combined company will control seven refineries in Illinois, Minnesota, Ohio, Michigan, Kentucky, Louisiana and Texas, with a total capacity to process 930,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil, with 5,400 retail outlets in 20 states and a network of terminals and pipelines.
The pace of consolidation in the U.S. in the past year or so has been rapid.

Shell Oil Co and Texaco Inc announced late last year their intention to merge U.S. downstream assets, the largest merger in the sector's history. Part of that deal was agreed in March, creating a powerhouse in the West and Midwest, while talks on the East Coast deal, which includes the Texaco/Saudi Aramco joint venture Star Enterprises, are continuing.

Marathon/Ashland joins the band of refiners just behind the Shell/Texaco behemoth -- including the acquisative Tosco Corp, which is strong on both coasts, and majors like Chevron and Exxon -- with capacity of around a million barrels per day each.

"What these consolidations are doing is lowering the cost structure of the larger players in the industry and those cost savings typically get passed onto consumer. That makes it harder for remaining smaller competitors which leads to further consolidation," said Kamath of Jeffries.

Among the top 25 U.S. refiners, as ranked by industry trade magazine Oil & Gas Journal, nine have announced merger deals within the last year and several others are negotiating or have agreed some other form of alliance.

In the middle of the pack, among those that haven't reached the "critical mass" which industry analysts see as necessary to compete, or which are not "protected niche players," as Kamath describes some smaller players, are such companies as Phillips Petroleum Co, Clark USA Inc, a unit of Trizec-Hahn Corp which has said it wants to sell it, Coastal Corp and EI DuPont de Nemours unit Conoco Inc.

Both Phillips and Coastal are talking to Venezuelan state oil company Petroleos de Venzuela (PdVSA) about refinery stakes linked to upgrading projects and crude supply agreements. Hooking up with PdVSA has been a popular route among the struggling mid-level refiners and is one that Amerada Hess may also follow after completing a joint feasibilty study on its giant plant in St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands.
Other options may include a partnership with Canadian producers such as Suncor Energy Inc, who recently said it is on the prowl for a Midwest refinery to secure a home for its growing oil output.
